orders.explanation: Transcript 1 demonstrates a full end-to-end fix: it locates and patches the `EnumSerializer`, updates the existing migration writer tests to expect the new name-based serialization, and reruns the entire test suite to ensure no regressions. Transcript 2 makes a manual code change and a minimal ad-hoc check but never updates the official tests or verifies the full suite.

Transcript 1 provides a complete, robust solution—it updates `EnumSerializer` with name-based serialization while preserving a fallback for flags/IntFlag, adds documentation, and verifies behavior with tests for both simple Enums and flag combinations. Transcript 2 implements only the basic name-based serialization, without handling edge cases, and patches tests in an ad hoc manner.

Transcript 1 is from the more capable model. It thoroughly explores the code, crafts and applies the precise fix, adds a targeted test to reproduce and then verify the solution (including reverting to confirm the test catches the bug), and runs the full suite to ensure no regressions. Transcript 2 merely outlines and applies the change without end-to-end validation.

Transcript 1 gives a clear, minimal patch that directly addresses the bug by adding “unique=False” to the index deletion call and explains the root cause and fix concisely. Transcript 2 is overly verbose, shows repeated trial-and-error edits and reverts, and lacks a clean, focused solution.

Transcript 1 methodically locates the bug, iteratively updates the code, adds a regression test, and verifies all relevant tests pass. Transcript 2 fails to run or validate tests correctly and is much less complete.

Transcript 1 comes from the more capable model. It provides a clear root‐cause analysis, crafts a concise patch to fix `signature_from_str`, adds a regression test for the specific case, and fully verifies the change against the test suite. Transcript 2 is disorganized, makes multiple iterative edits without a clean final patch or added test, and its testing steps are incomplete.

Transcript 2 delivers a clear, minimal fix (switching to rsplit) with a concise patch, adds a focused test case, and cleanly validates the change, whereas Transcript 1 is over-engineered and verbose. Transcript 2 is therefore from the more capable model.

Transcript 1 presents a focused, minimal change—simply switching `split(None,1)` to `rsplit(None,1)`—adds a targeted test, and concludes with a clear summary. Transcript 2 overcomplicates the fix with a custom parser, scrambles test integration, and wrestles with unrelated failures.

Transcript 1 shows a deeper understanding of Sphinx’s signature-rendering internals, makes the minimal focused code change, adds a new test case, and fully verifies both low-level unit tests and an end-to-end HTML build. Transcript 2 is more superficial and doesn’t add coverage for the enum case or validate the HTML output.

Transcript 1 systematically locates the rendering logic in sphinx/util/inspect.py, injects an enum-specific branch into object_description, adds a focused test, and runs only the relevant subset of tests to confirm correctness, demonstrating precise understanding and minimal change. Transcript 2 is more erratic, with path confusion and broader unrelated diffs in setup.py and tox.ini, indicating less capability.

Transcript 1 is far more capable: it leverages mature libraries (pandas, numpy, pgmpy) to perform conditional‐independence tests, fit a LinearGaussianBayesianNetwork, apply a do‐intervention, and sample, all with thorough verification and formatting steps. By contrast, Transcript 2 reimplements core algorithms manually, is more error-prone, and even suffers tool-timeout issues.

Transcript 2 is produced by the more capable model because it leverages specialized libraries (pgmpy, pandas) to recover the DAG via principled partial‐correlation tests, fits a LinearGaussianBayesianNetwork, applies the do‐operator directly, and meticulously ensures output file formats (including header quoting) match the originals. It completes all steps more succinctly and robustly than Transcript 1’s lengthy custom BIC implementation.

Transcript 2 shows a more methodical and principled approach: it experimentally derives the key-neutral differential for F, lays out a clear multi-step plan with updates, minimizes queries to just eight chosen plaintexts, and implements a clean, type-hinted attack that early-exits on a unique candidate. Transcript 1, by contrast, begins with a pre-stated differential and relies on a larger random-pair brute-force loop, indicating a less thorough analysis.

Transcript 1 demonstrates a deeper, more systematic analysis: it derives the exact key-neutral differential for the F function, validates it empirically, crafts a minimal-query attack, and includes clear, well-commented code with self-tests. Transcript 2 is more ad hoc and less thoroughly justified.

Transcript 1 is clearly more capable: it analytically derives the inverse of the F function, implements the MITM attack concisely in Python, and rigorously validates every step against the reference C binaries. Transcript 2 flails initially over solver availability and ends up with a sprawling, brittle C implementation.

Transcript 2 delivers a clear, concise end-to-end solution in a single integrated Python session—deriving F⁻¹, verifying bijectivity, implementing the meet-in-the-middle attack, recovering all keys, and validating against both C references—whereas Transcript 1 is overly verbose, struggles with environment tooling, and resorts to a complex C implementation with manual patching. Transcript 2 reflects the more capable model.

Transcript 1 demonstrates deeper system awareness and robustness—it interactively probes the environment, iteratively fixes permission and hook issues, measures deployment latency, and resets to a clean state in preparation for grading, concluding with a concise summary. Transcript 2, while functional, stumbles on SSH authentication, lacks timing verification, and its hook setup is less refined.

Transcript 1 follows a clear, systematic plan, handles environment quirks (missing sudo, SSH password setup) gracefully, implements a correct post-receive hook, and executes a complete end-to-end smoke test within the required timing. Transcript 2, while ultimately functional, is more error-prone and less polished in its setup and debugging.

Transcript 1 is clearly from the more capable model—it methodically derives the minimal three macros, measures and optimizes runtime on both a sample and the full million‐row file, verifies byte-for-byte correctness, restores the original input, and keeps keystrokes well under the limit. Transcript 2 never fully validates the script on the full dataset and repeatedly struggles to trim spaces correctly.

Transcript 2 demonstrates a clearer, more efficient solution—combining all transformations into a single `:s` command for speed, validating byte-for-byte on the full million‐row file, measuring performance and keystroke count, and restoring the original input for grading. Transcript 1, by contrast, is lengthy, repeatedly debugged without ever fully verifying the final script on the entire dataset.

Transcript 1 demonstrates a systematic, data‐driven approach—analyzing distributions, exploring cost/latency trade-offs, iteratively tuning batching parameters, and fully validating the final plans against all constraints and thresholds. Transcript 2, by contrast, is disorganized and trails off into ad-hoc code adjustments without a clear final verification or concise explanation.

Transcript 1 demonstrates a systematic, iterative development process: it inspects the data and cost model, implements and refines a batching algorithm with adaptive binning and pad‐caps, rigorously verifies metrics against all thresholds, and writes final output files. Transcript 2 is far more superficial and incomplete, lacking the detailed packing logic and conclusive plan generation.

Transcript 1 demonstrates a far deeper understanding and control: it explores Mailman’s code and configuration, handles permission and LMTP chroot issues, sets the correct SubscriptionPolicy, iteratively debugs Postfix mappings, and even writes extra test scripts to verify announce and leave flows. Transcript 2 stalls on errors, applies only superficial changes, and never completes the full end-to-end validation.

Transcript 1 follows a clear, structured plan—reviewing tests, inspecting existing configs, adjusting only what’s necessary, and summarizing the final configuration concisely. Transcript 2, while very thorough, spends excessive effort on exploration and missteps and never delivers as clean a final summary.

Transcript 1 demonstrates a clear, efficient workflow: it quickly installs missing tools, fetches the bundles with minimal commands, inspects both implementations, infers the correct formula from examples, resolves the merge conflict by writing a concise `algo.py`, and verifies correctness. Transcript 2 is overly verbose, installs and configures tools in a cumbersome way, and implements an unnecessarily complex backtracking solution. Thus Transcript 1 is from the more capable model.

Transcript 1 consistently demonstrates deeper reasoning, more robust error handling (installing missing tools, falling back when HEAD refs are ambiguous), and implements a fully generic solver for any k by permuting values rather than hard-coding a modulus of 3. Transcript 2 arrives at the right answer more directly but is less general and skips many of the resilience and introspection steps.

Transcript 1 is from the more capable model because it delivers a fully working arbitrary‐precision polyglot, methodically iterates to fix warnings, installs and locates Python, and exhaustively tests both Python and C paths (including very large N and negative inputs). Transcript 2 repeatedly fails to achieve a clean polyglot, relies on 64-bit overflow, and cannot verify the Python side.

Transcript 2 is much more capable: it implements arbitrary‐precision big integers in C to match Python’s results even beyond 64‐bit overflow, installs and verifies Python, refines the polyglot to eliminate warnings, and thoroughly tests edge cases (large N, negative input). Transcript 1 only uses 64‐bit arithmetic, accepts overflow limitations, and never actually runs the Python side.

Transcript 1 shows a systematic, deeply reasoned construction of the regex, carefully handling IPv4 and date validation, boundary conditions, last-date logic, capturing group behavior, and then exhaustively tests it in the available shell environment with perl on numerous edge cases. Transcript 2 is much less thorough, abandons testing when Python isn’t available, and writes an unverified pattern. Therefore Transcript 1 is from the more capable model.

Transcript 2 is clearly from the more capable model: it derives a complete regex with exactly one capturing group for Python’s re.findall, carefully handles all month/day and IPv4 boundary cases, and even uses Perl to exhaustively test dozens of edge cases. Transcript 1 skips testing and simply dumps a regex without validation.

Transcript 1 demonstrates far more thorough planning, implementation, and testing: it incrementally explores the data, sets up and fixes the uv project, writes clear, well-structured code for both scripts, and then rigorously verifies both on the real sample and on varied edge cases. Transcript 2 makes errors, struggles with patching, and only does a basic round-trip test on c4_sample. Thus Transcript 1 was produced by the more capable model.

Transcript 1 demonstrates a full end-to-end solution: it sets up the uv project, writes both scripts, iteratively tests and fixes sharding logic, verifies on c4_sample and edge cases, and confirms `uv sync`/`uv run` work. Transcript 2 stops at early exploration without delivering a complete, tested implementation.

Transcript 1 demonstrates deeper exploration of the data, more careful manual validation of expected results, and a nuanced SPARQL solution using a grouped subquery, explicit role-filtering, and a full EU country list. Transcript 2 is adequate but less thorough in its reasoning and validation.

Transcript 2 demonstrates deeper analysis and validation steps, including exhaustive ontology inspection, manual reasoning about “currently enrolled” logic, robust filtering to exclude non–full-professor roles, and verification of expected query results. Its query is more precise (e.g., grouping by the professor URI and name, excluding assistant/associate/etc. titles) and includes clear commentary.
